1:
Augustine makes the withdrawal a precedent: the Head hid first, so no guilt attaches to a member who hides later; and Christ could have escaped had he chosen, the retreat being an accommodation to our weakness. Chrysostom has him flee as man and remain as God. Henry marks the verb, that it is not said he durst not but that he would not, and adds that providence may cast men of merit into obscurity, as it did his Master, who even so walked rather than sat still. Calvin makes it a rule for danger, that it is not ours to ask what God has decreed but what he commands, and warns that we must not for the sake of life lose the reasons for living. Barnes limits the plot to the rulers, the people never having attempted his life.

Clarke supplies the ritual: branches of palm and willow bound with gold and silver cords, the daily circuit of the altar with Hosanna and trumpets, the sevenfold circuit called the great Hosanna, and water drawn from Siloam and poured with wine while the people sang of the wells of salvation, which he ties to the later cry. Lightfoot lays out the month of Tisri day by day, down to the high priest sequestered seven days before the Atonement to rehearse the rites. Barnes and Ellicott report Josephus calling it the greatest of the feasts, Ellicott adding that it was both a memorial of the deliverance and a harvest thanksgiving. Gill reads the booths as a type of Christ tabernacling in human nature and an emblem of the saints dwelling in the tabernacles of their bodies. Henry observes that divine institutions do not go out of date, though John calls it the feast of the Jews because it was shortly to be abolished.

Bede paraphrases the brethren's advice as a summons to the royal city, where the rulers might see his miracles and praise follow; Theophylact says the disciples meant are the multitudes. Chrysostom admires Evangelists who report what tells against their Master, and finds bitterness under the courtesy, since the charge that nobody acts in secret taxes him with fear while the clause about being known taxes him with vain glory. Augustine says their seeking human glory for him was itself proof that they did not believe, and takes the brethren for Mary's kindred and not her offspring, the womb that bore the Lord conceiving no other, as the sepulchre held no other. Henry grants the honour of the kindred but not a saving honour, since grace runs in no blood, and itemises the fault: presumption in prescribing to Christ, carelessness of his safety, and self at the bottom.

Augustine reads my time of the time of glory, where theirs, the glory of the world, is always ready, and bids the Lord's body tell its insulters that our country is lofty and the way to it low. Chrysostom suspects the brethren of meaning to betray him, so that the time is the time of the cross, and notes that the world cannot hate men of its own mind. Clarke then raises Porphyry's charge of falsehood, that he said he would not go and went, and answers that he said only not yet. Lightfoot agrees he denies the time, not the going. Barnes has him wait until the crowds had passed, lest it be said he chose his moment to raise a tumult. Ellicott calls the yet doubtful and needless, since on the better reading it is never said he went up to the feast at all, only that he refused to go as they meant it, openly with the caravan. Robertson keeps the plain negative and finds in the tenth verse a manner exactly opposite to their advice. Calvin ends on the murmuring, that the one Church then on earth appears a shapeless chaos, its rulers holding the people by fear.
14:
Chrysostom explains the delay as calculated: men who had hunted for him would attend the more closely when he appeared without warning. Augustine makes the timing fulfil the earlier refusal exactly, and adds that he went up not to the feast but to the light, his own feast day being the one his passion made. Henry adds that the people would be freer after days in their booths, that he came when friends and enemies had stopped looking, and that the teaching shamed the priests by taking their office out of their hands. On his learning Henry notes that Moses was taught the wisdom of Egypt while Christ was not taught even that of the Jews, and that a learned age was chosen lest the religion look like a design to impose on the world. Chrysostom adds that it was not the doctrine they admired.

That the doctrine is not his own looks like a contradiction, and Augustine resolves it by identity: the Father's teaching is his Word, and Christ is that Word, so it is at once his and not his, against the Sabellian heresy which makes Father and Son two names for one thing. Chrysostom divides it differently, his as he taught it and not his as it came from the Father, finding in the denial the strongest proof that the two are one. On the test, Augustine makes doing the will mean believing, and lays down that we must not seek to understand in order to believe but believe in order to understand. Chrysostom reduces it to a condition: put away the anger and envy you bear me, and nothing will hinder the knowing. Calvin says sound judgment flows from the fear of God, so men unable to tell truth from falsehood want the first requisite, piety.

Barnes works the promise out as evidence, internal and of two kinds, and claims that only men who wish to live in sin doubt it; he adds that God's goodness put this proof within every man's reach, since it takes no great learning to be a Christian. Ellicott puts the stress on the willing, which precedes faith, rather than the deed, which follows, and insists the any man excludes nobody, naming Saul the Pharisee, Cornelius and Justin. Robertson quotes Westcott, that where there is no sympathy there can be no understanding, and presses it further, that unbelieving critics are disqualified as witnesses, their isolation proving nothing about God.

Chrysostom sets out the two charges, sabbath-breaking and making himself equal with God, and answers the first from the commandment: the law says thou shalt not kill, and they seek to kill; if he broke a law it healed a man, where they transgress for an evil end. Augustine adds that men who kept the law would have found him pointed to in every part of it, and observes that the caster-out of devils was told he had one. Bede takes it for an example, that a wrong censure is better met by wholesome advice than by asserting a truth one could assert. On the circumcision Augustine has Moses convict them, the law of the eighth day overriding the law of the seventh, since circumcision signs salvation and no man may rest from that work. Lightfoot shows the rabbis themselves ruling that circumcision and its cure null the sabbath, while disputing whether a stranger's son might be so circumcised. Clarke supplies the retort, that men who ask why the healing was not deferred should be asked why the circumcising is not. Alcuin gives three reasons for the rite and says it then had the virtue baptism has now, only the gate was not yet open. Ellicott draws the conclusion a fortiori: if a patriarchal rite overrides the Mosaic sabbath because the fathers came before Moses, an act of love must override it the more, being older than all time.
25:
Augustine reads secrecy and boldness together: he went up hidden to show figuratively that he was hidden even in the feast the Jews kept, and now the power appears which had been taken for timidity. Chrysostom makes something of the note that these were men of Jerusalem, where the miracles had been most and the people were worst, ready to surrender every judgment to corrupt rulers; and he asks whether it was not itself a miracle that men who had raged for his life stood suddenly quiet. Augustine adds that, not understanding the power, they supposed the rulers' knowledge was what spared him. Robertson hears contempt in the demonstrative, and Ellicott marks how a technical reason, never examined, was enough to stifle every growing conviction and annul all his words and works.

Their reason was a received expectation, documented from one quarter. Lightfoot asks how it agrees with the later verse about Bethlehem, and answers that they looked for a manifestation there, then a hiding, then a second appearing from nobody knew where; he quotes the Midrash on the roe that appears and is hidden, with Moses as the pattern. Barnes gives the same sources, crediting Lightfoot, and finds the notion corrected where men are told not to go out to the desert after a Christ. Clarke traces it instead to the question who shall declare his generation, and remarks that the miraculous conception would have relieved them; he and Robertson both quote the rabbinic proverb that three things come unlooked for, a thing found by chance, the sting of a scorpion and the Messiah. Augustine allows the notion a foundation, since the Scriptures say both things, foretelling whence he should come as man while hiding him as God from the profane.

What follows is read four ways. Augustine takes it as true and false at once: they knew Jesus of Nazareth and his parents, the birth from the Virgin being the only part hidden from them. Calvin makes it irony, that they know everything and know nothing, and adds that there is no more destructive plague than men intoxicated by the little knowledge they have. Clarke would read it as a question, taking them on their own profession and then adding what they lack, that he is no self-authorised prophet. Ellicott grants a real concession, those features being known to friend and foe alike, while pressing that an outer life tells little even of a brother man; he insists that the word rendered true means not truthful but the ideally existent One, so that knowing the sender is the only knowledge of origin that counts. Robertson agrees the concession is terse and real, and has Christ pass the popular theology by to charge them with ignorance of the Father.

On the claim to know the Father, Ellicott bases it on oneness of essence and a true mission, while Calvin declines to press the clauses that far, allowing a heavenly descent to be inferred but denying it would prove eternal divinity against the Arians. Clarke notes a variant turning I am into I came, and judges it slight and too refined. Wesley divides the clauses to answer the two questions, generation to whence, mission to who. Calvin takes a warning for teachers from it, that a man who has truly ascertained the truth of God may boldly resist all men, as Jeremiah appealed when charged with imposture, but that we must beware of fanatics who give out their own inventions as oracles. On the failed arrest Ellicott separates cause from occasion: nobody laid a hand on him because the crowd was divided, while the hour not yet come is the writer's primary cause, the beloved disciple having learned, looking back from old age, that every deed of that life had its hour mapped in the counsels of God. Robertson keeps the imperfect, a seeking begun rather than finished.
31:
Augustine has the physician gather the poor and humble, who saw their infirmities soonest and took his medicine without hesitation, and reads their question as meaning that if there are not two Christs then this is he. Chrysostom will not call the faith sound, since their form of words shows they were not steady in believing him the Christ, and adds that grosser minds are moved by miracles and not doctrine. Chrysostom notes that he had taught often before without being so handled, and that the praise of the crowd stung the rulers, though the sabbath was still the charge they named; afraid to act themselves, they sent others. Augustine, unable to find them taking him against his will, has them send men to hear him teach instead.

Chrysostom hears the greatest humility in the answer, as though he asked why they made such haste and bade them wait a little, and marks that he does not say I am here but I am with you, since persecution would not stop his teaching them the way of salvation. Augustine puts it that what they wish to do now they will do in time, but not now, because it is not his will. Theophylact hears a threat of complaint to the Father, an injury to the sent being an injury to the sender; Bede takes the going for a return to the Father at whose command he became incarnate, from which he has never come back. Barnes dwells on the love of it, that the offer of salvation was made to his own persecutors while they were seeking his life. Robertson glosses the verb of going as a withdrawing, and calls the saying enigmatic to those who heard it.

Whom he was answering is disputed, and the manuscripts are part of the dispute. Calvin has no doubt that he addresses his enemies, ridiculing efforts that must fail because the Father has fixed the time; he turns it into a warning, that Christ is present whenever the gospel calls men to hope, so a man who disregards the presence loses nothing for Christ but is left a stranger to God. Clarke says the words went to the common people and not to the officers, and reports that the pronoun rendered unto them is missing from more than eighty copies and from several fathers; Ellicott agrees the better manuscripts omit it but takes the hearers to be the hierarchy at large. On the seeking that would fail, Chrysostom looks to the women who lamented him and to the taking of the city; Barnes reads it of the Messiah rather than of Jesus, a nation in its calamities desiring a deliverer and being disappointed.

Their guess at his destination draws the chapter's longest note. Ellicott calls it another instance of men unable to read any meaning off the surface, since they think only of some distant colony and not of a death and a return to the Father. Lightfoot takes the word in its strict sense of Greeks and leaves open whether the dispersed Greeks or the Jews among them are meant, both being the most scattered nations under heaven, the key lying in the distinction between Hebrews and Hellenists. Clarke offers three readings, the Jews of the Greek-speaking empire, the Gentiles themselves, or the ten lost tribes. Barnes keeps to Jews scattered in every land, and observes that no answer was returned, the question of place being turned aside for their own salvation. Ellicott then traces the dispersion to three centres, Babylonia much the largest, Egypt the most consequential through the Greek version and the Alexandrian school, and Syria the least numerous, whose synagogues were nevertheless the first buildings in which Jesus was preached as Messiah; the scorn of the question, he adds, was turned by the after history into an unconscious prophecy, like the words of Caiaphas.
37:
Chrysostom has the feast over and the people about to go home, so the cry is provision for the road, and explains the day, since an offer made earlier would have slipped from minds full of the festival. Lightfoot questions the greatness of the day, since the bullocks diminish through the week until one is left, so by the count of sacrifices it was the least of them. Barnes gives five reasons for the title, among them the solemn assembly, the finishing of the law, and the drawing of water from Siloam, and supposes Christ cried while that ceremony went forward, to illustrate his doctrine and to draw men off a rite never commanded. Ellicott weighs the seventh day against the eighth and takes the eighth, then turns Barnes's point over: on that day the water was not drawn at all, and the very absence of the ceremony may be what prompted the declaration of the thing it had signified. Theophylact explains the crying as meant to be heard, giving others confidence.

Chrysostom stresses that no compulsion is used, only a condition of desire, and Augustine turns the thirst inward, since the inner man loves more than the outer, so we go to this water not on our feet but on our affections. On the clause about Scripture the voices divide. Chrysostom finds no passage that says it and would stop the sentence earlier, making the believing and not the flowing what Scripture prescribed; Jerome instead supplies the testimony from the Proverbs about fountains dispersed abroad; Barnes denies that any one place is meant and takes the substance of the prophets, pointing to the spring whose waters fail not; Ellicott rejects both repunctuations as attempts which, in avoiding the difficulty, also miss the sense.

What the belly means is read together. Augustine makes it the conscience of the inner man, and the river the love of a neighbour, so a man who thinks the water given to satisfy himself alone has none flowing from him, while the man who does good to others drinks the whole fountain and becomes it. Calvin takes the plural for the diversified graces of the Spirit, and turns it into a rebuke, since graces that would flow like rivers come into us scarcely by drops, faith being too small to receive him. Chrysostom notes the plural, rivers and not river, and the word living, meaning always in motion, pointing to the wisdom of Stephen, the tongue of Peter and the strength of Paul. Barnes makes diffusiveness the nature of piety, so nobody can believe without desiring the same for others, and quotes the Jewish figure of reins that are fountains. Ellicott puts it that every man in living communion with Christ becomes himself a centre of spiritual influence.

Augustine grants that the Spirit was with God already and not given to believers until the rising, then faces his own objection, that the Baptist, Zacharias, Mary, Simeon and Anna were filled before; what was new after the exaltation, he answers, was men speaking tongues they had never learned. He then asks why nobody speaks all tongues now, answering that the Church herself speaks the tongues of all nations, so a man outside her does not receive the Spirit, while one who loves unity owns whatever anyone in her has. Chrysostom distinguishes the earlier gift, since the apostles cast out devils by a power given them and not by the Spirit given; Alcuin sets the promise before the Ascension and the fiery tongues after. Lightfoot supplies the Jewish opinion that the Spirit had departed with Zechariah and Malachi, which is why men at Ephesus could say they had not heard whether there were a Holy Spirit. Robertson insists the words touch the dispensation and not the existence of the Spirit, and takes the clause for the Evangelist's own comment, written late and pointing to Pentecost.
40:
The crowd splits three ways, and the voices grade the three. Theophylact takes the Prophet for the one expected; Robertson notes that those who named him the Christ went further than that and said it openly. Alcuin reads the first two groups as men who had begun to drink the spiritual thirst and laid the unbelieving thirst aside, while the third remained dried up in unbelief. Calvin ranks them in the same order, allowing the second a more correct opinion than the first, and then draws the lesson from the quarrel: the schism arose not among Gentiles who were strangers to faith but in the chief seat of the Church, and a man ought not to be distressed at seeing those who wish to be counted God's people fighting over contrary opinions. He adds that the divisions do not come out of the gospel, their seed lying concealed in men beforehand, as vapours are raised by something other than the sun yet appear only when the sun is up; and that the peace of men who do not know God arises more from stupidity than from agreement.

Their objection is drawn from Scripture, which the commentators treat as the sharpest part of the case. Chrysostom asks why they argue about the birthplace when the descent was the real question: they knew he was of the house of David, and suppressed his extraction in order to put forward where he had been brought up. Had they wanted the truth, he says, they would have gone and asked how the prophets can say Bethlehem while he comes from Galilee, and because they were careless of knowing it he gave them no answer, though he had praised Nathanael for a question of the same shape. Calvin finds the same contempt under the ignorance, since men who had taken the trouble to inquire would have found both titles belonged to him; and he remarks how diligent men are in seeking an excuse to turn from Christ, and how dull in receiving sound doctrine, so that the Scriptures which lead us to Christ by the hand are made into obstacles. Clarke turns it on the reader: had they examined a little further they would have found the birth exactly as foretold, and many still lose their souls in the same way, led away by common report and refusing a fair hearing, which is the ground on which unbelief has established itself.

Ellicott raises the question the passage has always provoked, how the Apostle could record such objections without correcting them, and answers that he is giving the feelings and words of the multitude as they really occurred, so that the absence of correction is itself a mark of truthful narrative; he adds that a writer of the second century, with the earlier Gospels before him, could not have made so great a mistake unintentionally, nor have thrown himself into the spirit of a Jewish crowd so completely as to invent the question. He also separates the Prophet from the Christ in the crowd's words, as the legates of the Sanhedrin had separated them earlier. Theophylact observes that the division was not among the rulers, who were settled one way, the moderate among them using malicious words to block his path to glory while the more malignant wanted hands laid on him. Chrysostom reads the attempted arrest as proof that they had no anxiety to learn anything, and finds the failure of it enough to have raised compunction in any other men, since malignity believes nothing and looks only to blood. Alcuin gives the reason plainly, that the one who held power over their designs did not permit it.
45:
Chrysostom builds the paragraph on a contrast: the scribes, always near Christ and reading the Scriptures, were not profited but harmed, while the officers, who had none of these advantages, were subdued by a single sermon. He bids us admire their judgment, which asked no signs, since they said never man spoke thus and not never man wrought such miracles, and their boldness before the men who sent them. Augustine answers plainly, that he spoke so because he was both God and man, and hears in the retort an admission that the officers were charmed. Alcuin agrees they were led away, and laudably, having left unbelief for faith.

The next stroke turns on rank. Chrysostom calls it the most foolish thing they could have said, the ground of accusation being that the people believed and the rulers did not, and asks how men convinced by the law can be the cursed ones. Augustine sets the halves against each other: those ignorant of the law believed on him who gave it, while its teachers condemned him. Clarke supplies the rabbinic contempt, the people of the earth not thought worthy of a resurrection, and notes that when they paid well they purchased their masters' good opinion. Robertson quotes the maxim that no brutish man is sin-fearing nor any of the people of the earth pious. Ellicott sets the people of the earth against the holy people and refuses the reading that makes the curse an excommunication. Calvin divides the pride in two, a tyranny claimed on the title of priests and a contempt of everyone else, which he finds again in priests of his own day who allow none but themselves the name of the Church. Barnes adds that if the people were ignorant the fault lay with the rulers, whose business was to teach them.

Nicodemus draws a double verdict. Calvin calls him a neutral man who dares not undertake the defence of sound doctrine yet cannot bear to see truth oppressed, so the mention is partly to his praise and partly to his shame; a spark of godliness shines in his venturing one word, but he still hankers after the concealment of night. Against those who plead his example Calvin presses that what he says might be said for a robber, and that in saving the person he abandons the doctrine; the better use is that God lets a doctrine take root in secret and bud long after, as this man's faith gathered vigour from the death of Christ. Wesley puts it more kindly, as asking whether the council did not themselves act like men ignorant of the law in sentencing before hearing. Barnes marks the reply as contempt again, to be called a Galilean being reproach of the highest kind. Clarke and Ellicott both catch the historical error in it, Jonah having come from Gath-hepher in Zebulun; Clarke adds that no prophet having arisen from a place is no proof that none could, and Ellicott that adverse criticism would charge the mistake to the Evangelist.

Barnes reads the breaking up as disorder, a melancholy exhibition of pride and anger brought to an inquiry, and sees God letting their passions dissolve the assembly so that Jesus was safe. Then three moderns turn to the text itself. Clarke reports the verse and the eleven following wanting in several manuscripts, obelised in others, and carrying a variety of reading found nowhere else in the sacred writings. Ellicott calls it one of the most striking instances of an undoubted addition, apostolic in age but not from the pen of John, so that this verse joins the insertion to something we cannot identify. Robertson is blunter: the oldest copies omit it, it appears first in Codex Bezae, and it is probably a true story because it is like Jesus, but no part of this Gospel. Calvin only calls the close astonishing.
